Vignette:
# Fariha's Watch

Fariha was fifty-three when she first called the therapist, her voice steady on the phone but her hands trembling as she held the receiver. She was a ship captain—had been for twenty-eight years—commanding container vessels across the Atlantic with a reputation for precision and unflappable judgment. Yet for the past three years, something had begun to unravel in the quiet hours of her own home, and she could no longer explain it away as the wear of the job.

The abuse had started when she was four. Her father, a man whose moods shifted like weather, had raised his hand to her for small infractions—a spilled glass of milk, a question asked at the wrong moment, the simple fact of her presence when he wanted silence. The violence was not constant, which made it somehow worse; she learned to read the angle of his shoulders, the particular silence that preceded his rage. By the time she was old enough to leave, at twenty-one, she had internalized a simple truth: safety was an illusion, and the people who were supposed to protect her—her mother, who looked away; the school nurse who asked no follow-up questions; the relatives who knew and said nothing—had failed her completely. That failure had calcified into something harder than anger: a certainty that she could rely on no one but herself.

She had built her life around this knowledge. The sea became her refuge. On a ship, the hierarchy was clear, the rules were written, and she was in command. No one could hurt her without facing consequences. She had married Karim twenty-five years ago, a good man who loved her, though she maintained a careful distance even from him, a wall she told herself was just her nature. They had no children—she had not wanted them—and she had gradually drifted from the Lebanese community in her city, telling herself she was too busy, that she had outgrown those ties, though the truth was more painful: being around families, around mothers and daughters, stirred something in her that she could not name.

Three years ago, during a shore leave, something shifted. She was alone in the house one evening when she heard a car door slam outside. The sound—ordinary, meaningless—had sent her body into a state of alarm so acute that she could not breathe. She had found herself on the kitchen floor, her heart racing, and she could not remember how she had gotten there. What followed was a slow, creeping colonization of her peace. At night, she began listening for sounds—the creak of the house settling, the distant hum of traffic—interpreting each one as a potential threat, a sign that someone was coming. She would lie awake, her ears straining, her body rigid, unable to relax even when Karim slept soundly beside her and the house was locked and dark. The nighttime became the worst part; daylight brought a fragile sense of safety, but as soon as the sun began to set, dread would settle in her chest.

She had tried to manage it on her own. When the memories came—sometimes just a flash of an image, her father's hand raised, his face contorted—she would push them away, clench her jaw, think of something else, anything else. Other times, the memory would come without the image: a wave of terror and shame and helplessness, as if her body remembered what her mind refused to show her. And then there were the strange, dissociative moments when she could recall the facts of what had happened with perfect clarity but feel absolutely nothing, as if she were describing something that had happened to someone else entirely.

The consequences had been quiet but cumulative. She had begun making excuses to take shorter contracts, reluctant to leave Karim for weeks at a time, though she could not quite articulate why. She had stopped attending the annual community dinner that had been a fixture of her life. She had started having drinks before bed to force herself into sleep. And in the past year, she had begun to ruminate obsessively about the past—about how things might have been different if she had been quieter, more obedient, less of a burden; about who she might have been if none of it had happened; about the person she used to be before the hypervigilance and the fear had become her baseline. She found herself thinking, *If only I had known then what I know now. If only someone had stepped in.*

It was Karim who finally insisted she get help. He had found her one morning standing in the kitchen at three in the morning, having not slept, listening to the house. "This is not living," he said quietly. "This is surviving. Let someone help you." She came to the first session afraid that talking about it would make it worse, but also afraid that she could not go on like this—caught between a past she could not escape and a present in which she could not feel safe, even in her own home, even in the company of someone who loved her.
